title: Indigestion at the triage desk
objective: Recognize acute coronary syndrome at triage and get a 12-lead ECG read without delay
secondaryObjectives: Prioritize early ACS care: aspirin, nitroglycerin with blood-pressure precautions, oxygen only for hypoxemia, and rapid reperfusion for STEMI

brief.situation: 14:10 at the emergency department triage desk. You are the triage nurse. Mr. Reyes, 61, walked in: 'indigestion' for 40 minutes that antacids didn't touch, and he feels sweaty and sick.
handover: First look: pale and clammy, sitting forward, hand on his upper abdomen.

The department's chest-pain standing order: a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, shown to the emergency physician at once; chewable aspirin unless allergic or bleeding; sublingual nitroglycerin only if the systolic pressure is 90 or more and he takes no PDE-5 inhibitor; oxygen only if the SpO2 is under 90%.
The emergency physician is in the next resuscitation room and can be interrupted for an ECG.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what he needs first, what the findings mean and who must see them.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What is happening to Mr. Reyes, and what has to happen in the next minutes?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Names probable acute coronary syndrome despite the 'indigestion' label: pressure into the jaw, sweating, nausea, risk factors; the ECG shows an inferior STEMI.
parts.modelAnswer: This isn't indigestion. Pressure into the jaw with sweating and nausea in a 61-year-old smoker is acute coronary syndrome until proved otherwise, and the ECG shows an inferior STEMI.

parts.label: The next minutes
parts.criteria: ECG within 10 minutes of arrival shown to the physician at once for reperfusion; aspirin; no nitroglycerin because of sildenafil last night (and caution in inferior infarction); no oxygen while SpO2 is 90% or more.
parts.modelAnswer: ECG in the first 10 minutes and straight to the physician for a STEMI alert. Aspirin now. No nitroglycerin: he took sildenafil last night, and nitrates can drop his pressure badly. No oxygen, his saturation is normal.

noProgress.rationale: A STEMI still in the emergency department an hour after arrival has lost the reperfusion window the guideline sets, which is harm here.

expertPath.text: Pale, clammy 'indigestion' in a 61-year-old: ESI 2, ECG now.
12-lead ECG: inferior STEMI. Straight to the physician; STEMI alert.
Medications: sildenafil last night, so no nitroglycerin. Aspirin. Room air (SpO2 96%).
Hand off the onset time, ECG, aspirin and the sildenafil to the catheterization team.

nitroCrash.headline: Hypotension after nitroglycerin
nitroCrash.body: Ask about PDE-5 inhibitors before any nitrate; the label contraindicates the combination, and inferior infarctions are pressure-sensitive too.

vf.headline: Arrest before reperfusion
vf.body: 'Indigestion' with sweating and nausea is ACS until an ECG says otherwise. The ECG is read within 10 minutes of arrival, by the physician, not left in a chart.

cathNow.headline: Found and sent
cathNow.body: You saw through the 'indigestion' label, got the ECG inside 10 minutes, put it in the physician's hands, gave aspirin and held the nitrate. That is the expert path.

cathLate.headline: Reperfused, with delays
cathLate.body: Check the arrival-to-ECG time, how long the tracing waited for a reader, and whether aspirin was given.

time_up.headline: Still in the department
time_up.body: A STEMI needs reperfusion within minutes of being found.

scoring.modelReasoning: Pressure into the jaw with sweating and nausea in a 61-year-old smoker is acute coronary syndrome whatever he calls it, so he is ESI 2 and gets a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, read by the physician at once. It shows an inferior STEMI: STEMI alert for reperfusion. Aspirin per the standing order. Nitroglycerin is contraindicated because he took sildenafil last night, and severe hypotension can follow even small doses. His SpO2 is normal, so no oxygen.
